title: Meet the tones
description: Learn what tone marks mean before building your first phrases.
objectives: Recognize the four written tone marks.
Notice that tones change in connected speech.
explanation: In Mandarin, pitch patterns help distinguish words. Pinyin marks the four tones: mā (high and level), má (rising), mǎ (low, with a possible rise), and mà (falling). These are a guide to pitch, not four different volume levels.
A third tone is often low without a full dip and rise inside a phrase. When two third tones meet, the first is usually pronounced like a second tone: 你好 is written nǐ hǎo but commonly spoken ní hǎo.
A neutral-tone syllable is short and unstressed; its pitch depends on the preceding tone. These questions check tone concepts. They do not measure your spoken pronunciation or acoustic tone accuracy.

examples.meaning: Mum — first tone: high and level.
Tea — second tone: rising.
Water — third tone; its shape depends on context.
Be — fourth tone: falling.
Mum — the second syllable is neutral in this common pronunciation.

questions.prompt: Written-tone check: which tone is high and level?
questions.explanation: The first tone is high and level. The mark ā is a reminder of a level pitch.
questions.hint: Look for the horizontal tone mark.

questions.prompt: Written-tone check: the mark in chá represents which pattern?
questions.explanation: The acute mark á represents the second, rising tone.
questions.hint: The mark slopes upward.

questions.prompt: Written-tone check: which syllable has a fourth tone?
questions.explanation: The mark ì slopes downward and denotes the fourth tone.
questions.hint: Find the downward-sloping mark.

questions.prompt: In ordinary speech, how is the first tone of nǐ hǎo usually pronounced?
questions.explanation: Before another third tone, the first third tone normally changes to a rising second tone. Dictionary pinyin still writes nǐ hǎo.
questions.hint: This phrase places two third tones together.

questions.prompt: Which description fits a neutral-tone syllable?

options.text: Short and unstressed; pitch depends on context

questions.explanation: Neutral tone is not a fixed fifth pitch contour. It is unstressed and changes with context.
questions.hint: Think of the second syllable in māma.

title: First connections
description: Say hello, thank someone, and turn a statement into a question.
objectives: Understand common greetings.
Use 吗 at the end of a yes-or-no question.
explanation: 你好 (nǐ hǎo) is a useful beginner greeting. 谢谢 (xièxie) means “thank you”, and 不客气 (bú kèqi) is a common reply meaning “you are welcome”. Use 再见 (zàijiàn) to say goodbye.
Add 吗 (ma) at the end of a statement to make a yes-or-no question. 你好吗？ asks “How are you?” literally “Are you well?”; it is a useful learning example, not the only natural way to greet someone.
Pinyin below usually shows dictionary tones. Some examples show the spoken form: 不 is normally pronounced bú before a fourth tone, as in 不客气. Do not judge every syllable in isolation.

Thank you.
You are welcome. (Spoken tone change on 不.)

questions.explanation: 你好 is the greeting “hello”. Its first syllable changes tone before the second third tone.
questions.hint: The two characters literally relate to “you” and “good”.

questions.explanation: 不客气 is a common reply to 谢谢.
questions.hint: Choose the expression that tells someone there is no need to be polite.

questions.prompt: Build: “Are you well?”
questions.explanation: The statement 你好 becomes a yes-or-no question when 吗 is added at the end.
questions.hint: Put the question particle last.

questions.prompt: Where does 吗 go in this kind of yes-or-no question?
questions.explanation: 吗 follows the whole statement. The original word order stays the same.
questions.hint: Think of 你好吗？

questions.prompt: Choose the expression for “goodbye”.
questions.explanation: 再见 means “goodbye”, literally suggesting seeing someone again.
questions.hint: It is the expression used when leaving.

fact.title: A very old writing tradition
fact.text: Shang rulers recorded questions and outcomes on animal bones and tortoiseshells. These oracle-bone inscriptions preserve early Chinese written records, including questions about rain and hunting.

title: This is me
description: Introduce yourself and build your first complete statements.
objectives: Introduce your name and identity.
Place a time expression before the action.
explanation: 我 means “I” and 你 means “you”. Use 叫 for a name: 我叫安娜 means “My name is Anna”. Use 是 before a noun describing an identity: 我是学生 means “I am a student”.
你叫什么名字？ asks “What is your name?” Here 什么 already asks “what”, so do not add 吗. 安娜 is an example name, not a required translation of your own name.
A basic action sentence follows subject → verb → object: 我学习汉语. A time expression such as 今天 goes before the verb, either before or after the subject: 今天我学习汉语 / 我今天学习汉语.

questions.hint: 叫 introduces a name.

questions.explanation: 今天 goes before 学习. It can appear before or after 我, so both time placements are accepted.
questions.hint: Keep 今天 before the action.

questions.explanation: 吗 creates a yes-or-no question; 什么 already asks for the missing information.

title: People around me
description: Talk about family, possession, and things people like.
objectives: Use 的 for a possessive phrase.
Say who someone is and what they like.
explanation: 爸爸 means “dad” and 妈妈 means “mum”. 我的妈妈 means “my mum”: the owner comes first, then 的, then the person or thing. With close family, 的 is also often omitted, as in 我妈妈.
他 and 她 are written differently but both are pronounced tā. 是 introduces an identity, while 有 means “have”. When counting people, 一个 is a basic number-classifier combination.
喜欢 means “like”. Put 也, meaning “also”, before the verb: 妈妈也喜欢茶. A neutral second syllable in bàba or māma should not be treated as a full fourth or first tone.

questions.explanation: In the full possessive form, the owner 我 comes before 的 and 妈妈. 我妈妈 is also natural, but this exercise supplies 的.
questions.hint: Owner → 的 → person.

questions.explanation: 她 is the subject, 是 links the identity, and 老师 is teacher.
questions.hint: Person → 是 → identity.

questions.explanation: The pattern is 妈妈也喜欢茶: 也 comes before the verb 喜欢.
questions.hint: 也 modifies the following action.

questions.hint: Finish 我喜欢茶 first, then add the clause about Dad.

title: Tea, please
description: Ask for a drink and describe what you do or do not drink.
objectives: Build subject–verb–object sentences.
Use 想 and 不 before the action.
Recognize a quantity phrase for a drink.
explanation: 喝 means “drink”. Start with the subject, then the verb, then the drink: 我喝水. 想 before the verb expresses wanting to do something: 我想喝茶 means “I would like to drink tea”.
不 goes before the verb to negate a habitual action or present intention: 我不喝茶 means “I do not drink tea”. Here 不 is bù because 喝 has a first tone; before a fourth tone it normally changes to bú.

For a drink, 一杯水 means “one cup of water”: number → container measure → drink. 杯子 is the noun “cup”; 杯 is the measure used in this phrase. 一 has dictionary tone yī but is pronounced yì before the first tone of 杯.

questions.explanation: 我想喝茶 ends in 茶: the speaker wants tea.
questions.hint: 茶 is chá.

questions.explanation: The subject 我 comes before 喝, and the object 水 follows it.
questions.hint: Who → action → drink.

questions.prompt: Build: “I would like to drink tea.”
questions.explanation: 想 goes before the action 喝: wanting to drink tea.
questions.hint: Place 想 immediately before 喝.

questions.prompt: What does 我不喝茶 mean?
questions.explanation: 不 negates 喝, while 茶 remains the object.
questions.hint: 不 is the negative word.

questions.prompt: Build: “one cup of water”.
questions.explanation: Put the number first, then 杯 as the container measure, then the drink 水.
questions.hint: Number → cup measure → drink.

title: Finding your way
description: Practise 从 … 到 … in a short, connected elementary lesson.
objectives: Use 从 … 到 … in context.
